issues.legal_issue: Land is a forest for acquisition purposes only if it meets the ordinary meaning of forest or the applicable statutory extension of that meaning.
material_facts: The land was treated in the underlying proceedings as land that had been appropriated or brought under cultivation before the relevant statutory cutoff, and the State had acknowledged that it was not forest land.
The disputed lands had been built upon over time for residential, industrial, or commercial use.
issues.conclusion: The disputed lands did not fall within the ordinary or extended meaning of forest and therefore were not forests under the acquisition statute.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of forest in Section 2(c-i) of the Maharashtra Private Forests (Acquisition) Act, 1975 begins with the ordinary meaning of forest; the inclusive part extends, but does not displace, that meaning. The Court relied on Waghmare v. State of Maharashtra, Jagir Singh v. State of Bihar, Black Diamond Beverages v. Commercial Tax Officer, and the interpretive principle discussed in Robinson v. Barton-Eccles Local Board and Craies on Statute Law.

predicates.forest_acquisition_proceeding: A proceeding determines whether land is a forest for purposes of statutory acquisition.
predicates.land_does_not_meet_ordinary_or_extended_: The land lacks the features of forest under the ordinary meaning and does not fall within an applicable statutory extension of that meaning.

issues.definition: When an acquisition proceeding concerns land that does not meet either the ordinary or extended meaning of forest, the land is not a forest for acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A notice under the forest-protection procedure triggers the statutory category for private-forest acquisition only when it is served on the landowner, not merely issued or published.
material_facts: A notice under Section 35(3) was published in the official gazette, but it was not served on the landowner.
The applicable procedure provided for service on the owner, publication, an opportunity to object, and consideration of objections; the notice also imposed restrictions carrying penal consequences.
issues.conclusion: The word “issued” in Section 2(f)(iii) of the acquisition statute must be read in context to include service; mere issuance or gazette publication of an unserved notice was insufficient.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(f)(iii) and 35(3)–(5) require service so that the owner can object and be heard, and so that notice of restrictions with penal consequences is given. The Court overruled Chintamani Gajanan Velkar v. State of Maharashtra to this extent, explaining that it had not considered the applicable amendments to Section 35. It applied the contextual approach to interpretation supported by R.L. Arora v. State of U.P., Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar, and Joginder Pal v. Naval Kishore Behal; it also distinguished the treatment of “issue” in Banarsi Debi v. ITO and CWT v. Kundan Lal Behari Lal.

predicates.private_forest_acquisition_proceeding: A proceeding determines whether land falls within a statutory category of private forest for acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_claim_relies_on_forest_prote: The claimed private-forest status depends on a notice issued under a forest-protection procedure.
predicates.notice_not_served_on_owner: The notice was not served on the landowner, even if it was issued or published.

issues.definition: In a private-forest acquisition proceeding based on a forest-protection notice, the notice does not trigger the relevant statutory category if it was not served on the owner.

issues.legal_issue: A stale forest-protection notice that was not decided within a reasonable time cannot support acquisition of land as a private forest.
material_facts: The notice was issued many years before the acquisition statute came into force, and no decision was made on it for about eighteen years.
The State did not take possession or act on the notice, while it permitted construction and other development on the land over many years.
issues.conclusion: The notice had become a dead letter and was not a live notice capable of supporting private-forest status under the acquisition statute.
issues.legal_principle: Where a statute prescribes no time for exercising a power or deciding a notice, it must be exercised or decided within a reasonable time. The Court relied on Ramlila Maidan Incident, In re, Mansaram v. S.P. Pathak, and Santoshkumar Shivgonda Patil v. Balasaheb Tukaram Shevale. It also held that the acquisition provision must be construed strictly because it effects expropriation, relying on Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, State of M.P. v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, and Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan.

predicates.private_forest_acquisition_proceeding: A proceeding determines whether land falls within a statutory category of private forest for acquisition.
predicates.notice_left_undecided_beyond_reasonable_: The authority did not decide the notice within a reasonable time in the circumstances.
predicates.state_did_not_act_on_notice: The State did not pursue the notice or take steps to implement it.

issues.definition: A notice left undecided beyond a reasonable time and not acted upon by the State cannot support private-forest status in an acquisition proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: Demolition is not an appropriate remedy for extensive construction where the State’s prolonged inaction and permissions led citizens reasonably to rely on the legality of the development.
material_facts: The State and its authorities granted permissions for extensive construction and provided infrastructure over many years, without attempting to take possession of the land.
Numerous buildings were constructed and occupied, including by residents who had invested in homes, and the State’s later position would have required demolition and displacement on a large scale.
There was no allegation that the State had acted arbitrarily or irrationally to confer a voluntary benefit on the builders; the construction followed the legal process and official permissions.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the land was private forest, the State could not demolish the extensive existing constructions in the circumstances of these appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Although unauthorized construction that is not legally compoundable is generally liable to be demolished, the remedy is not applied automatically in every case; its application depends on the facts and practical consequences. The Court distinguished K. Ramadas Shenoy v. Chief Officer, M.I. Builders v. Radhey Shyam Sahu, Pleasant Stay Hotel v. Palani Hills Conservation Council, and Pratibha Coop. Housing Society Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra, which involved materially different circumstances, including deliberate or flagrant violations. The Court emphasized State responsibility, citizens’ reliance on official permissions, and the extraordinary scale and duration of the development.

predicates.forest_land_demolition_dispute: A dispute concerns whether construction on land claimed to be forest should be demolished.
predicates.extensive_construction_occurred_over_man: A substantial amount of construction was completed and occupied over an extended period.
predicates.state_permitted_or_enabled_development: State authorities granted permissions or provided infrastructure while development proceeded.
predicates.citizens_reasonably_relied_on_state_cond: Citizens invested in or occupied the development in reliance on the State’s permissions, conduct, or prolonged inaction.

issues.definition: In a forest-land demolition dispute, extensive long-term construction is not to be demolished when the State permitted or enabled the development and citizens reasonably relied on its conduct.
